content: RUB A535, also known as Antiphlogistine, is a topical analgesic that was first introduced in 1919. It is manufactured by Church and Dwight in Canada. While it is relatively unknown outside of Canada and is not sold in the United States, it is a widely popular product within Canada for the treatment of various conditions, including severe muscle pain, arthritic pain, rheumatic pain, bursitis, and lumbago. According to Church and Dwight, nearly all research, development, and production of RUB A535 have been conducted in Canada and continue to be based there. Patients who have allergies to salicylates, such as those found in aspirin or other ASA-based drugs, should avoid using RUB A535. Additionally, individuals taking anticoagulant medications are advised against using this product due to potential contraindications. Initially, RUB A535 was available as a white cream with a strong medicinal odor. More recently, the product line has expanded to include dual-action back patches, known as Hot-Cold patches, which provide alternating temperature sensations. An improved version of the cream has also been developed, marketed as odorless, in contrast to the original cream, which retains the characteristic smell of most topical analgesics. The product is sometimes referred to simply as A535, a shorthand that appears to be primarily used within Canada. For French-speaking consumers in Canada, the product is marketed under the name Antiphlogistine. There are anecdotal reports of RUB A535 being used in unconventional ways, including during sexual activities. According to entries on SlangDictionary.com, the product has been associated with practices referred to as Spicy Stranger or Fire and Ice. In these scenarios, RUB A535 is applied to the penis or scrotum to induce a warming or burning sensation. In the Fire and Ice variation, an ice cube is first used to cool or stimulate the genitals, followed by the application of RUB A535 to create a warming effect. However, these uses have not been medically confirmed or endorsed. A similar practice in the United States involves the use of Ben-Gay on the genitals, which is reportedly considered highly uncomfortable, particularly among athletes in locker room settings.
